data.interpretation: The KPI asks to maximize the number of orders delivered town-wide within the promised pickup and delivery times. It explicitly allows revising those promised times (a DELIVERY_SLA contract change, which a human must decide). Any change that is worse for customers must be justified by its measured effect on them. On-time count is the main measure, but it depends on the promise itself, so customer impact has to be tracked with measures that do not depend on the promise: actual wait times and orders left undelivered. The KPI states no numeric levels, so no targets or guard values are set.

options.label: Maximize town-wide on-time deliveries, monitoring customer wait

goals.text: Number of orders delivered within the promised times across the town (higher is better)
Customers' 95th-percentile wait from order to delivery, which does not depend on the promise; monitored so that SLA loosening that worsens real service is visible
Orders still undelivered at the end of the period; monitored as the clearest customer harm
Longest single customer wait; monitored for worst-case customer impact

options.note: Literal reading of the KPI. Every SLA revision still goes to a human, who reviews the monitored wait-time and unfinished values before accepting it. No guard values are set because the KPI gives no levels.

options.label: Improve customers' actual wait time, monitoring on-time deliveries

goals.text: Customers' 95th-percentile wait from order to delivery (lower is better); cannot be improved by loosening promises
Orders delivered within the promised times; monitored so the promises are not neglected
Orders undelivered at period end; monitored

options.note: Uses a promise-independent measure as the primary goal, so a contract change cannot count as improvement just by relaxing deadlines. This drifts from the KPI's literal wording, which counts on-time deliveries.

concerns: Proxy risk: on_time_deliveries is measured against the promised times. If those times are loosened, the count can rise while customers actually wait longer. Wait-time and unfinished metrics are monitored to expose this, but the human must weigh them when judging any SLA revision.

The KPI requires a reason, based on measured effect, for any customer-worsening change, but it sets no level of acceptable worsening. No guard thresholds are set. If the human wants a hard limit (e.g., a maximum p95 wait), it must be stated.
Under the same random seed the number of orders is fixed, so on_time_deliveries and on_time_rate rank changes identically. The count was chosen to match 'as many orders as possible'.
